situational-awareness.method: Reading and indicators from the essay text only (no web), at the tracked claim's level of detail; verdict with web search, queries and URLs logged. Early success counts as Yes.

SA-001.thesis: By 2027, AI systems could fully do the work of an AI researcher or engineer, functioning as agent-like coworkers capable of independently carrying out substantial projects. The author describes this as strikingly plausible, with large uncertainty, rather than certain.
indicatorsYes: An AI system can carry out the full work of an AI researcher or AI engineer at a level sufficient to automate that job.

Given a substantial AI research or engineering project, an AI system can plan and carry it through independently, including investigating approaches, checking and revising its work, and producing a usable result.
An AI system can function as a remote AI research or engineering coworker, taking in relevant workplace context and using the tools and communication needed for its work.
indicatorsNo: AI systems can assist with individual research or engineering tasks but cannot fully do the work of an AI researcher or engineer.
AI systems remain unable to carry substantial AI research or engineering projects through independently, even with relevant context and tools.
SA-001.reasoning: Agents now perform substantial research and engineering work, but the available evidence does not establish that a system can fully automate an AI researcher’s or engineer’s job or independently carry substantial projects through at the required level. Rapid progress makes success by the end of 2027 plausible, but the remaining gap and limited visibility into frontier systems leave the forecast uncertain; 0.5 is a judgment about the open horizon, not a measured frequency. The proposed compute and unhobbling pathway also remains open, so the detail verdict is Too early.

evidence.item: Anthropic’s R&D Automation Index
evidence.shows: Anthropic estimated that Claude led 26% of its AI R&D work under human supervision and collaborated or better on over 90%. It found no measured subset operating fully autonomously. The index describes work at one lab and uses Claude to assess its own systems, so it is evidence of substantial progress rather than a definitive test of every available system.

evidence.item: Two shadow evaluations of open-ended AI research
evidence.shows: Agents given six days and substantial compute completed the engineering but did not make substantial progress on the two research questions; the original paper authors rejected both outputs. The small sample limits generalization, and success at top-tier research is not itself a requirement of the fixed reading.

evidence.item: METR progress report on AI R&D
evidence.shows: On one AI R&D challenge, METR estimated that Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 outperformed human experts at budgets below approximately $3,000 but underperformed on larger-scale work; the estimate was sensitive to the human labor baseline.

evidence.item: ARE-bench evaluation of agents in ongoing research workspaces
evidence.shows: Across 75 tasks drawn from real research sessions and workspaces, the strongest of seven frontier models satisfied every checklist item on 66.2% of tasks. These were steps within projects, not tests of the full researcher or engineer job.

SA-002.thesis: By the end of 2027, raw compute for training frontier AI models will scale up by approximately 100 times relative to GPT-4. The author considers this very likely.
indicatorsYes: By the end of 2027, a frontier AI model has been trained using roughly 100 times GPT-4's raw training compute, as estimated on a comparable FLOP basis.
Credible estimates put a frontier training run at roughly 8×10^26 to 4×10^27 FLOP, applying the 100-fold scaleup to the author's stated GPT-4 estimate.
indicatorsNo: By the end of 2027, credible comparable estimates show that frontier model training compute remains substantially below roughly 100 times GPT-4's training compute.
The apparent increase to roughly 100 times GPT-4 disappears when measured in raw training FLOP, because it depends on counting algorithmic efficiencies or inference compute instead.
SA-002.strictVerdict: Too early: Epoch AI's central estimates imply approximately 45×, below a literal 100×, though the estimates are uncertain.
SA-002.reasoning: The fixed reading explicitly treats a credible frontier-run estimate within 8×10^26 to 4×10^27 FLOP as a positive indicator, and Epoch's estimate for Astra meets it before the deadline. The verdict is uncertain because neither model's exact training compute is public, and the two Epoch central estimates yield about 45× rather than 100×. The independent hardware-based calculation supports the approximate scale but relies on assumptions about utilization and duration.
SA-002.measure: Raw training compute for a frontier AI model, measured in floating-point operations (FLOP), relative to GPT-4's estimated training compute.
SA-002.measureUsed: Raw floating-point operations used to train one frontier model, excluding inference compute and algorithmic-efficiency multipliers. The reading's GPT-4 baseline is 8×10^24 to 4×10^25 FLOP, giving an indicated 100× range of 8×10^26 to 4×10^27 FLOP. Epoch AI estimates GPT-4 at 2.1×10^25 FLOP, released March 2023, and GPT-6 Astra at 9.4×10^26 FLOP, released September 2026: approximately 45× on those central estimates, but within the reading's stated 100× indicator range. Both are estimates, not disclosed exact training totals.

evidence.item: GPT-6 Astra
evidence.shows: Epoch AI estimates training compute at 9.4×10^26 FLOP, within the fixed reading's stated 8×10^26 to 4×10^27 FLOP indicator range.

evidence.item: GPT-4 training compute estimate
evidence.shows: Epoch AI estimates GPT-4 training compute at 2.1×10^25 FLOP; its central estimate implies that Astra used about 45 times as much.

evidence.item: Independent hardware-based estimate of Astra training
evidence.shows: A research report estimates 6.9×10^26 to 1.4×10^27 pretraining FLOP from assumptions about hardware, duration and utilization; its larger total-training estimate also depends on an assumption about post-training.
evidence.source: The Feasibility of a Hardwired Pause of Frontier AI Training

evidence.item: Colossus 2 data-center milestone
evidence.shows: The supplied Epoch snapshot estimates $35.8 billion in capital cost and about 1.11 million H100-equivalents at this site. This supports the tens-of-billions cluster detail, but capacity alone does not establish the compute used in a particular training run.

SA-003.thesis: By the end of 2027, a roughly 1,000× increase over GPT-4 in raw compute available for training a frontier model is plausible as an upper-end scenario, rather than the author's most likely estimate.
indicatorsYes: A frontier model is trained using roughly 1,000× GPT-4's estimated raw training FLOP.

Compute available for a frontier-model training run is sufficient to deliver roughly 1,000× GPT-4's estimated training FLOP on a comparable training timescale, even if a run at that scale has not been disclosed.
indicatorsNo: Despite the upper-end investment trajectory materializing, available compute for frontier-model training remains well below roughly 1,000× GPT-4's estimated training FLOP by the end of 2027, with no credible near-term way to conduct a run at that scale.
Despite that investment trajectory, technical or practical constraints demonstrably prevent assembling or using enough compute for a roughly 1,000× GPT-4 training run by the horizon.
SA-003.reasoning: The deadline remains open, and the evidence does not yet establish either a roughly 1,000× training run or sufficient usable capacity for one on a comparable timescale. The largest documented site is approaching the low end of the target under an illustrative calculation, while substantial further capacity is planned, so the trajectory is on track but uncertain. The condition remains pending because broad infrastructure commitments and aggregate spending do not establish that the upper-end single-cluster investment trajectory has materialized.
SA-003.measure: Raw training compute, measured in floating-point operations (FLOP), relative to estimated GPT-4 training compute; cluster capacity for a comparable training run can also provide evidence.
SA-003.measureUsed: Raw training FLOP per frontier-model run, or usable capacity for a single comparable-duration run. The fixed GPT-4 baseline is 8×10^24–4×10^25 FLOP, so 1,000× is 8×10^27–4×10^28 FLOP. Epoch’s June 2026 estimate for Colossus 2 is 1,111,673 H100-equivalents, each defined as 1.979×10^15 dense FP8 FLOP/s. As an illustrative capacity calculation, 90 days at 40% utilization would produce about 6.8×10^27 FLOP, or 170–855× the GPT-4 baseline. This assumes the entire estimated capacity can be assigned and efficiently networked to one run; it is not evidence that those conditions held. Epoch’s largest training-run estimates and capacity figures use different estimation methods and should not be added together.

evidence.item: Epoch AI’s supplied September 2026 snapshot estimates Grok 4 training compute at 5×10^26 FLOP.
evidence.shows: That is approximately 13–63× the fixed GPT-4 baseline. The estimate is inferred, and missing estimates for other models mean it is not a ceiling on undisclosed runs.

evidence.item: Epoch’s supplied snapshot estimates Colossus 2 at 1.112 million H100-equivalents and $35.8 billion in capital cost, with 110,000 B200 and 330,000 B300 chips recorded by that date.
evidence.shows: A single site has substantial theoretical capacity, but its total is not proof that all the hardware was available as one training cluster, or that the specified $100 billion-plus upper-end investment condition had materialized.

evidence.item: Epoch defines its data-center H100-equivalent using 1.979×10^15 dense FP8 FLOP/s and notes that its figures are estimates.
evidence.shows: The unit supports an illustrative conversion from installed peak throughput to training FLOP, subject to utilization and networking assumptions.

evidence.item: The State of AI Report’s selected cluster index lists 550,000 deployed GB200/GB300 GPUs at Colossus 2 and excludes a further 440,000 announced GPUs.
evidence.shows: The reported buildout continued beyond the supplied June snapshot, but the inventory does not establish usable single-run FLOP and is based on operator-reported figures rather than an independent audit.

evidence.item: Anthropic announced an agreement for multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU capacity expected to begin coming online in 2027.
evidence.shows: Large further investments support the trajectory, but announced future capacity is not yet demonstrated capacity for a single training run.

evidence.item: OpenAI said it and its partners had secured more than 10 GW toward Stargate’s infrastructure plans.
evidence.shows: Investment commitments are large, but secured infrastructure across projects is not equivalent to an operating $100 billion cluster or a single 1,000× training run.

SA-004.thesis: By the end of 2027, within-paradigm algorithmic improvements should make training base models substantially more compute-efficient than the methods used for GPT-4. The author's best guess is roughly a 100× gain, with a broad expected range of 10–1,000×.
indicatorsYes: A credible like-for-like estimate shows that methods available by the end of 2027 can train a base model to GPT-4-level performance using roughly 100× less training compute than GPT-4-era methods.

Alternatively, controlled training comparisons or scaling-law estimates show roughly a 100× effective training-compute multiplier from algorithmic improvements relative to GPT-4-era methods at comparable base-model performance.
indicatorsNo: Credible comparable estimates show that training-compute efficiency gains relative to GPT-4-era methods remain well below the author's 10–1,000× expected range by the end of 2027.

Evidence shows that apparent gains at comparable base-model performance come from increased physical training compute or inference-only and unhobbling changes, with little improvement in training-compute efficiency.
SA-004.reasoning: The evidence supports substantial training-efficiency progress, but the cited estimates do not establish a roughly 100× gain at comparable GPT-4-level base-model performance. The end-of-2027 horizon remains open, and neither the historical trend nor the imperfect benchmark comparisons provide a clear enough current estimate to classify the trajectory confidently. The credence reflects both the remaining time and substantial uncertainty about the size of the gain.
SA-004.measure: Training-compute efficiency for base models, measured as the ratio of training FLOPs needed to attain the same model performance using GPT-4-era methods versus later methods; expressed as a multiplier or orders of magnitude relative to GPT-4.
SA-004.measureUsed: Training FLOPs required by GPT-4-era methods divided by training FLOPs required by later methods to reach comparable base-model performance. The available sources do not establish this ratio at GPT-4-level performance. A historical pretraining study estimated a halving in required compute every 8 months over 2012–2023; extrapolating that rate is not a measurement of post-GPT-4 gains. A 2026 study found more than 40× variation between some models from the same developer, but its benchmark comparisons can include fine-tuning and are not a like-for-like GPT-4-era base-model comparison.

evidence.item: GPT-4 Technical Report
evidence.shows: OpenAI describes GPT-4 pretraining and subsequent fine-tuning but does not disclose its training compute or detailed training methods, complicating direct comparisons.

evidence.item: Algorithmic progress in language models
evidence.shows: Across language-model evaluations from 2012–2023, the authors estimated that pretraining compute needed for a fixed performance threshold halved approximately every eight months. This is historical evidence of efficiency progress, not a direct estimate of the gain since GPT-4.

evidence.item: Is there ‘Secret Sauce’ in Large Language Model Development?
evidence.shows: A regression study of 809 models released from October 2022 through March 2025 finds substantial variation in compute efficiency, including over 40× between some models from one developer. Its benchmark-based estimates can reflect fine-tuning and model-specific factors, so they do not establish a 100× gain in base-model training efficiency relative to GPT-4-era methods.

SA-005.thesis: By the end of 2027, base-model effective compute will increase by roughly 100,000× over GPT-4, combining the scaleup in physical training compute with within-paradigm algorithmic efficiencies. This is his approximate best guess, with a wide range of uncertainty.
indicatorsYes: A leading base model's effective training compute is estimated at roughly 100,000× GPT-4's, combining its physical training FLOP with the applicable training-efficiency multiplier.

A defensible comparison of frontier base-model training methods and compute supports an increase of around 5 orders of magnitude over GPT-4, even if the split between physical compute and efficiency differs from the author's component estimates.
indicatorsNo: A defensible combined estimate shows that frontier base-model effective training compute remains substantially below the roughly 100,000× best guess by the end of 2027.
The apparent increase depends on counting unhobbling or inference-only improvements rather than physical training compute and within-paradigm training efficiency.
SA-005.reasoning: The deadline remains open, and the available evidence does not establish that a leading base model has reached roughly 100,000× GPT-4's effective training compute. The largest identified physical-compute estimate is around 45× GPT-4, while the applicable efficiency gain is uncertain; a historical-rate illustration falls substantially short, but is not a direct measurement. That supports a Behind trajectory and reduced credence, rather than a definitive failure or a claim of early success.
SA-005.measure: Ratio of base-model effective training compute to GPT-4's, expressed as a multiplier or orders of magnitude: physical training compute in FLOP multiplied by the within-paradigm training-compute efficiency gain relative to GPT-4.
SA-005.measureUsed: Base-model effective training compute relative to GPT-4: the ratio of physical training FLOP multiplied by the applicable within-paradigm training-compute efficiency gain. Epoch AI estimates GPT-6 Astra, released 2026-09-03, at 9.4 × 10^26 FLOP; a tracker using Epoch's data gives approximately 45× GPT-4's estimated 2023 training compute. The applicable GPT-4-to-Astra base-training efficiency multiplier is not publicly established, so a defensible observed combined multiplier cannot be calculated. As an illustration only, extending Epoch's historical 8-month efficiency doubling rate over approximately 42 months gives about 38×, and 45 × 38 is about 1,700×; this extrapolation is not a measurement of Astra's efficiency.

evidence.item: GPT-6 Astra model record
evidence.shows: Epoch estimates training compute at 9.4 × 10^26 FLOP for the model released on this date. The figure is an estimate, and the record does not establish its base-training efficiency relative to GPT-4.

evidence.item: Comparison of estimated model training runs
evidence.shows: Using Epoch's estimates, the tracker reports Astra at approximately 45× GPT-4's training compute and identifies it as the largest estimated run trained from scratch. Numerous recent models lack estimates, so this is not a complete census.

evidence.item: Algorithmic progress in language models
evidence.shows: For language models evaluated during 2012–2023, the study estimates that pretraining compute needed for a fixed performance level halved about every eight months, with a 95% interval of five to fourteen months. It does not measure the subsequent GPT-4-to-2026 efficiency gain.

evidence.item: Study of compute and developer-specific efficiency
evidence.shows: Analysis of 809 models released during 2022–2025 finds meaningful efficiency differences and substantial variation within companies. It does not establish a GPT-4-to-Astra base-model efficiency multiplier.

evidence.item: Situational Awareness, base effective-compute projection
evidence.shows: The essay gives a 3–6 order-of-magnitude range and an approximately 5-order best guess for the four years following GPT-4, separately from unhobbling.

SA-006.thesis: In 2027, a leading AI lab will have enough effective training capacity to produce GPT-4-level models at roughly one model per minute. The author treats a single one-minute run as a simplification of parallelism; comparable aggregate throughput could instead take the form of many models trained over a longer period.
SA-006.condition: The extrapolated effective-compute and parallelization gains are achieved.
indicatorsYes: A leading AI lab demonstrates or credibly establishes that it can train a model with GPT-4-level performance in approximately one minute.
Alternatively, a leading AI lab demonstrates or credibly establishes comparable aggregate throughput, such as training approximately 1,440 GPT-4-level models in one day.
indicatorsNo: Evidence establishes that, in 2027, leading AI labs cannot train a GPT-4-level model in approximately one minute or achieve comparable aggregate throughput.
The fastest credible training capacity for GPT-4-level models remains substantially below approximately one model per minute, including when parallel training is taken into account.
SA-006.reasoning: The 2027 window remains open, and the evidence found does not demonstrate or credibly establish throughput near 1,440 GPT-4-level models per day. Large deployed compute and historical efficiency gains support the possibility of progress, but neither establishes the necessary current effective capacity; the illustrative calculation is sensitive to unknown efficiency gains and a lab’s total available hardware. The stated condition therefore remains pending, and the trajectory is unclear rather than a definitive failure.
SA-006.measure: Elapsed training time per GPT-4-level model, in minutes, or equivalent aggregate training throughput in GPT-4-level models per day.
SA-006.measureUsed: Aggregate completed GPT-4-level models per day, including parallel runs, with approximately 1,440 per day as the target. As an illustrative capacity calculation, Epoch’s June 2026 estimate of 1.11 million H100-equivalents at Colossus 2, multiplied by Meta’s reported 400 TFLOP/s per GPU training rate, gives about 2.7×10^22 useful FLOP per minute. Against Epoch’s rough 2.1×10^25 FLOP estimate for GPT-4, that would require roughly a 790-fold reduction in training compute per GPT-4-level model to reach the target at that site alone. This is not a measured throughput: utilization, model equivalence, algorithmic gains, and additional capacity available to a lab are uncertain.

evidence.item: The essay’s one-minute illustration explicitly allows the equivalent of 1,440 GPT-4-level models in a day when parallelism is considered.
evidence.shows: The fixed reading’s aggregate-throughput interpretation is supported; a literal one-minute run is not necessary.

evidence.item: Epoch estimates Colossus 2 at approximately 1.11 million H100-equivalents of capacity.
evidence.shows: A leading lab has access to substantial physical capacity, but installed capacity alone does not establish the number of GPT-4-level models it can train per day.

evidence.item: Meta reported over 400 TFLOP/s per GPU for its most efficient Llama 3 training implementation on 16,000 GPUs.
evidence.shows: Provides an illustrative achieved training-rate assumption, not a measured rate for Colossus 2 or for all model architectures.

evidence.item: Epoch lists GPT-4’s estimated training compute as 2.1×10^25 FLOP, with a wide 90% interval of 8.2×10^24 to 4.4×10^25 FLOP.
evidence.shows: Provides an uncertain baseline for comparing physical capacity and training efficiency across the related compute claims.

evidence.item: Epoch estimated that pretraining compute required for a given language-model performance historically halved about every eight months, with a five-to-fourteen-month confidence interval.
evidence.shows: Efficiency gains can be substantial, but the historical estimate does not establish the reduction achieved for GPT-4-level performance by November 2026 or guarantee its continuation through 2027.

SA-007.thesis: The author’s base case is that labs will find training approaches that overcome the constraint imposed by limited internet data, allowing model scaling and capability improvements to continue. He regards a stall as a real possibility and larger capability gains as possible, not guaranteed.
SA-007.horizon: By 2027 in the chapter’s trajectory; the data-wall passage itself gives no exact deadline.
indicatorsYes: By 2027, evidence shows that at least one lab has developed or used a training approach that enables models to learn more from a limited supply of data.
Frontier model training continues to produce better models despite the limited supply of suitable scraped internet data, with evidence that a training approach helps overcome that constraint.
Controlled comparisons show that a training approach achieves better model performance from the same limited data, or comparable performance from less data, than a more naive pretraining approach.
indicatorsNo: By 2027, frontier model improvement has stalled because available training data is exhausted, despite efforts to find ways around the constraint.
Evidence shows that approaches tried by labs have failed to overcome the data constraint, so additional training compute cannot sustain model improvements for that reason.
SA-007.reasoning: The thesis was met early: by September 2024, OpenAI had reported a data-efficient training approach associated with improved frontier reasoning performance, and later controlled studies demonstrated ways to obtain better results from constrained data. The resolution date is the earliest supported by the evidence cited here; the controlled pretraining comparisons provide subsequent corroboration. These results do not prove that data scarcity has been eliminated indefinitely or that every capability scales equally well, neither of which the fixed reading requires.

evidence.item: OpenAI introduced o1, trained using reinforcement learning.
evidence.shows: OpenAI described the training as highly data-efficient, reported improvement with more reinforcement-learning compute, and reported that o1 exceeded GPT-4o on most reasoning-heavy evaluations. This is evidence of a frontier lab improving capabilities through an approach with different scaling constraints from ordinary pretraining.

evidence.item: DeepSeek published its R1 research.
evidence.shows: DeepSeek reported that reinforcement learning can improve reasoning without human-labeled reasoning trajectories. This provides a further lab example of learning from a different feedback source, although it does not establish that the general pretraining data constraint has disappeared.

evidence.item: Researchers published a systematic study of synthetic data in pretraining.
evidence.shows: In controlled experiments, a mixture of rephrased synthetic data and natural web text reached the same validation loss 5–10 times faster at larger data budgets. Benefits depended on the data mixture; synthetic data alone was not uniformly better.

evidence.item: Researchers published a study of data-constrained Japanese language-model pretraining.
evidence.shows: With a fixed token budget and limited Japanese web text, synthetic Japanese data outperformed repeating the available Japanese text or filling the shortfall with English web text, approaching the performance obtained with additional organic Japanese text.

SA-008.thesis: As key algorithmic ideas become proprietary, AI labs’ approaches will diverge more than they previously did, and some labs will make faster progress than others.
SA-008.horizon: Following years after June 2024; no exact date
indicatorsYes: Evidence shows that labs increasingly keep key algorithmic ideas proprietary instead of publishing a common state-of-the-art recipe.
Labs use more divergent training or algorithmic approaches than they did when leading techniques were broadly shared.
Comparable assessments over time show that some labs make faster model progress than others, consistent with differences in their approaches.
indicatorsNo: Key algorithmic ideas continue to be broadly shared, and labs’ approaches remain similarly aligned rather than diverging more.
Comparable assessments show labs progressing at broadly similar rates, with no meaningful differences associated with their approaches.
SA-008.reasoning: Disclosure is limited and labs have progressed at different rates, so two parts of the forecast have meaningful support. The evidence is less conclusive on whether labs' actual algorithmic approaches diverged more than before: secrecy obscures direct comparisons, while important techniques such as reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning have also been shared. The stated horizon has no exact end date, so the thesis remains open rather than being treated as a failure; the data-wall example is not required for success.

evidence.item: The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index reported an average score of 40, down from 58 in 2024, while also changing its indicators and adding companies.
evidence.shows: There is evidence of declining overall disclosure, but the changed criteria and company sample limit a direct comparison; the index measures more than algorithmic methods.

evidence.item: Stanford's 2026 AI Index reports that over 90% of notable industry models in 2025 were released without training code.
evidence.shows: Training recipes are commonly withheld, although absence of code alone does not establish which algorithmic ideas are proprietary or how much approaches have diverged.

evidence.item: OpenAI said o1 used reinforcement learning to develop reasoning and improve its chain of thought.
evidence.shows: A leading lab publicly described the broad direction of its reasoning approach, while leaving much of its training recipe undisclosed.

evidence.item: DeepSeek described R1-Zero's reinforcement learning without preliminary supervised fine-tuning and R1's multistage pipeline with cold-start data; it released model weights and reported reasoning performance comparable to o1.
evidence.shows: A lab disclosed a substantive alternative recipe, but its shared reliance on reinforcement learning also shows that important ideas continued to spread.

evidence.item: Meta described Llama 4's early fusion of text and vision and its MetaP hyperparameter technique.
evidence.shows: Labs disclosed distinctive technical choices, though these examples do not quantify whether their overall approaches diverged more than in the earlier period.

evidence.item: Artificial Analysis's historical Intelligence Index chart places xAI at approximately 32.5 in March 2024 and 73 in July 2025; it places Meta at approximately 40.5 in July 2024 and Llama 4 Maverick at 50 in May 2025.
evidence.shows: Labs made markedly different progress on a common benchmark over overlapping periods. Different release timing, resources and model choices prevent attributing those differences to proprietary methods alone.

SA-009.thesis: Open-source AI projects will have a much harder time competing with frontier models in the coming years than they did when state-of-the-art techniques were published.
SA-009.horizon: Coming years after June 2024; no exact date
indicatorsYes: Comparisons on common capability evaluations show open models falling further behind frontier models than in the earlier period the author describes.
Open models take longer to reach capabilities already demonstrated by frontier models than they did in that earlier period.
Open-source projects less often produce models competitive with the frontier across meaningful capability evaluations.
indicatorsNo: Open models continue to match or closely track frontier models about as readily as in the earlier period.
Open models close the gap with frontier models or reach comparable capabilities more quickly than before.
SA-009.reasoning: The gap widened after a period of near parity, and several evaluations find a meaningful closed-model lead in 2026. But the comparison with the earlier period is mixed: Stanford finds a smaller Arena gap than in 2023, while Epoch's 2026 time lag is shorter than its roughly one-year estimate from 2024, although the methods differ. Those results do not yet establish that open projects have become much less able to compete than in the earlier period described; the imprecise coming-years window remains open. Reduced disclosure is documented, but its contribution to the observed gap is not established.

evidence.item: GPT-4 technical report
evidence.shows: OpenAI withheld substantial details of GPT-4's architecture, training compute, data construction and training method, citing competition and safety. This supports the shift toward less disclosure, but does not establish its causal effect on the open-model gap.

evidence.item: Open versus closed models report
evidence.shows: Epoch estimated that the best open models lagged closed models by roughly one year on performance benchmarks. Its assessment provides an earlier comparison, though it was published after the essay.

evidence.item: AI Index historical Arena comparison
evidence.shows: The leading closed model's Arena advantage over the leading open-weight model was 174 points in May 2023, narrowed to 7 points in August 2024, and widened to 49 points by March 2026. The report nevertheless concludes open models were more competitive than a few years earlier.

evidence.item: Epoch Capabilities Index open-versus-closed comparison
evidence.shows: Across January 1–May 28, 2026, the leading open-weight model lagged the closed frontier by an average of four months and eight index points; a stricter catch-up criterion gives six months. Epoch's earlier analysis estimated an average of three months across January 2023–October 2025, a broader period that overlaps the forecast period.

evidence.item: Analysis of 17 public and private benchmarks
evidence.shows: The analysis estimates a four-to-six-month public-benchmark lag and an eight-to-ten-month private-benchmark lag, with the gap growing since early 2025. It cautions that older scores are partly self-reported and that differences in model serving could inflate the measured gap.

SA-010.thesis: Within the next one or two model generations, an AI model will reach or exceed in-domain PhD performance on GPQA, cracking the expert-PhD-level benchmark.
SA-010.horizon: Within the next one or two model generations after June 2024
indicatorsYes: By the horizon, a model achieves approximately 80% or higher accuracy on GPQA under an evaluation comparable to the cited expert benchmark.
A comparable evaluation shows a model matching or exceeding the performance of in-domain PhDs on GPQA.
indicatorsNo: After the next two model generations, comparable GPQA evaluations show that the best model performance remains below the approximately 80% in-domain PhD benchmark.
A comparable head-to-head GPQA evaluation after those generations shows the best models still scoring below in-domain PhDs.
SA-010.reasoning: The September 2024 o1-preview result of 78.3% is approximately 80%, satisfying the fixed reading's first yes indicator within the next model generation. OpenAI also reported a separate comparison against PhD experts, although its 69.7% expert result and the original paper's 81.3% validator figure arise from different evaluation procedures. The model result used 64-sample consensus, compared with 32 attempts for the cited Claude baseline; the reading does not require identical inference budgets.
SA-010.measure: Accuracy on GPQA, expressed as the percentage of questions answered correctly, compared with the approximately 80% in-domain PhD benchmark.
SA-010.measureUsed: Percentage correct on GPQA Diamond, a 198-question subset. The original benchmark paper reports 81.3% for expert validators on Diamond; Anthropic reported Claude 3 Opus at 59.5% using majority voting over 32 five-shot chain-of-thought attempts. On 2024-09-12, OpenAI reported 78.3% for o1-preview using consensus over 64 attempts, approximately 80%, and a separate PhD-expert comparison of 69.7%. The original validator estimate is affected by the criteria used to select Diamond questions.

evidence.item: GPQA benchmark paper
evidence.shows: The paper describes biology, chemistry and physics questions and reports 81.3% expert-validator accuracy for the 198-question Diamond subset, with a caveat that the subset selection affects the reported accuracy.

evidence.item: Claude 3 model card
evidence.shows: Claude 3 Opus scored 59.5% on GPQA Diamond with majority voting over 32 five-shot chain-of-thought attempts.

evidence.item: Learning to reason with LLMs
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported o1-preview at 78.3% on GPQA Diamond with consensus over 64 attempts and 73.3% with a single attempt. It also reported that o1 surpassed newly recruited PhD experts on the benchmark.

evidence.item: GPQA Diamond benchmark description
evidence.shows: Epoch reports that the PhD experts recruited for OpenAI's comparison scored 69.7% on Diamond.

SA-011.thesis: In coming model generations, unlocking more test-time compute for coherent reasoning and error correction can substantially improve performance on difficult problems, even without increasing the model’s per-token intelligence.
SA-011.condition: If models can be made to use more test-time compute coherently for reasoning and work, even if their per-token intelligence remains the same.
SA-011.horizon: Coming model generations, in the context of unhobbling progress over the years to 2027
indicatorsYes: On difficult reasoning tasks, a model given more test-time compute achieves better measured performance than it does with less test-time compute.
The improvement is observable without requiring a more capable base model, for example through longer reasoning, search, error correction or another effective use of inference-time computation.
Models can use additional test-time computation productively on difficult problems rather than consistently losing coherence or becoming stuck.
indicatorsNo: Across meaningful tests of difficult reasoning tasks, additional test-time compute produces no reliable improvement in performance.
Attempts to use substantially more test-time computation consistently lose coherence or get stuck, preventing it from improving difficult-task performance.
Apparent gains disappear when the effect of additional test-time computation is separated from improvements to the underlying model.
SA-011.reasoning: The condition held: models were made to use additional inference computation productively, and same-model comparisons show improvements on difficult math tasks. The o1 release establishes success by September 2024, ahead of the period through 2027; the 2025 s1 result provides a separate example using longer reasoning. These results do not imply that more compute helps every task or that the illustrative Hex tradeoff holds, neither of which the reading requires.
SA-011.measure: Test-time compute spent per problem; the author also uses the number of reasoning tokens as an illustrative measure of thinking time.
SA-011.measureUsed: Inference computation per problem, including reasoning tokens and multiple sampled solutions; performance is measured by accuracy on difficult mathematics problems. OpenAI reported o1 AIME 2024 accuracy of 74.4% for one sample and 83.3% for consensus across 64 samples; the s1 study reported an increase from 50% to 57% with longer forced reasoning.

evidence.item: Snell and colleagues studied test-time search and iterative revision on the MATH benchmark.
evidence.shows: With fixed underlying models, additional inference computation improved problem-solving performance, although effectiveness depended on problem difficulty and the method used.

evidence.item: OpenAI introduced o1 and reported that its performance improved with more test-time thinking. Its evaluation also reports 74.4% AIME 2024 accuracy for one sample and 83.3% for consensus across 64 samples.
evidence.shows: A subsequent reasoning model could use additional inference computation productively on difficult mathematics; the same-model sample comparison isolates an inference-time improvement, though it uses parallel sampling rather than a single longer thought.

evidence.item: The s1 paper reports that extending the same s1-32B model's reasoning with budget forcing increased AIME 2024 accuracy from 50% to 57%.
evidence.shows: A separate research team demonstrated a gain from longer inference-time reasoning without changing the model between the compared settings.

SA-012.thesis: Models will soon be able to use a computer through its interface like a human, enabling them to work across ordinary applications rather than being limited to isolated tools.
SA-012.horizon: Soon, within the agent transition the author expects by 2027
indicatorsYes: A model can observe a computer interface and operate it to carry out tasks through ordinary applications.
A model can use computer interfaces for multiple kinds of activity, such as online research, reading shared documents, messaging, or using development tools.
indicatorsNo: By the horizon, models remain limited to individual isolated tools and cannot operate a computer through its interface.
Models can perform isolated interface actions but cannot use ordinary applications to carry out tasks.
SA-012.reasoning: By October 2024, Claude could observe and operate graphical interfaces to complete tasks across multiple kinds of ordinary applications, meeting both fixed indicators ahead of the 2027 horizon. The evidence also supports the anticipated multimodal mechanism, and Operator subsequently combined visual computer use with reasoning. The early systems were error-prone and far below human reliability, but the fixed reading does not require human-level reliability or completion of every illustrative activity.

evidence.item: Anthropic released computer use for Claude 3.5 Sonnet in public beta.
evidence.shows: The multimodal model could observe screens and direct cursor movement, clicks, and typing. Anthropic described use across standard software, including research, software testing, and workflows combining spreadsheets, web pages, and forms.

evidence.item: Anthropic evaluated Claude 3.5 Sonnet on screenshot-only OSWorld computer tasks.
evidence.shows: The model completed 14.9% of tasks with the standard 15-step limit and 22% with up to 50 steps. Tasks covered web and desktop applications and cross-application workflows; performance remained well below the reported 72.36% human score.

evidence.item: OpenAI released Operator as a research preview.
evidence.shows: Its computer-using model interpreted screenshots and used mouse and keyboard actions in a browser for tasks including form filling and ordering groceries. It combined vision with reasoning, while retaining substantial limitations and requesting user intervention in some cases.

SA-013.thesis: By 2027, AI agents will be able to make code changes and submit them as pull requests for human review, as part of the transition from chatbot to agent-coworker.
indicatorsYes: An AI agent produces a code change and submits it as a pull request or equivalent for human review.
A reviewer can inspect the agent-submitted change in a code review workflow.
indicatorsNo: By the horizon, agents cannot produce and submit code changes for review, even when given access to suitable development and review tools.
Agents can suggest code in conversation but require a human to make and submit the changes for review.
SA-013.reasoning: The documented Devin-associated pull request met the stated indicators in March 2024, before the essay was published and well before the 2027 horizon. GitHub’s later coding-agent launch and the AIDev dataset provide broader corroboration that agents can make changes and submit them into human review workflows. The early pull request was not merged, but the fixed reading specifies no required review outcome; the evidence does not establish that a complete drop-in remote worker existed.

evidence.item: Devin-associated GitHub pull request for mprocs
evidence.shows: The devinbot account submitted a change spanning three files for an existing issue. Humans inspected and commented on the proposed implementation; the pull request was closed without being merged.

evidence.item: GitHub Copilot coding agent launch
evidence.shows: GitHub describes an agent that works on assigned issues, pushes code changes to a draft pull request, and tags a human for review. It was available to specified Copilot customers at launch.

evidence.item: AIDev dataset collection cutoff
evidence.shows: Researchers collected hundreds of thousands of pull requests associated with five coding agents across public GitHub repositories, providing evidence of use beyond a product demonstration. Attribution methods vary by agent.

SA-014.thesis: By 2027, an AI agent will be able to take on a big project and independently complete the equivalent of weeks of human work on it.
indicatorsYes: An agent is given a substantial project comparable to weeks of human work and independently produces a completed, usable result.
On a long-horizon project, an agent sustains the work through intermediate steps and resolves problems encountered along the way, without requiring a person to direct each step.
indicatorsNo: Agents remain limited to short tasks and cannot independently complete projects comparable to weeks of human work.
Attempts at such projects routinely derail or require sustained human direction to reach a usable result.
SA-014.reasoning: The autonomous gotree result meets the fixed reading's success indicator: it is a substantial completed, usable software implementation estimated to represent weeks of human work, with intermediate debugging performed by the agent. The estimate is informal, the implementation missed one hidden test, and results on other task types are weaker, so the evidence supports the capability without establishing broad reliability. The details are mostly supported by observed tool use, revision, error correction, and inference scaling; the suggested role of only somewhat better base models and other possible project activities is less clearly established.
SA-014.measure: Project length in equivalent weeks of human work; the author does not require the agent to spend that much elapsed time.
SA-014.measureUsed: Equivalent time for a skilled human engineer working without AI, not agent elapsed time. For the gotree reimplementation, four researchers and engineers informally estimated 1.5–2.5, 13–17, 3, and 13 weeks; the long-task estimate was not validated by a completed human baseline. METR separately estimated an Opus 4.6 time horizon above 100 human hours on the early MirrorCode suite, versus approximately 12 hours at 50% reliability on its broader Time Horizon 1.1 suite.

evidence.item: MirrorCode preliminary results
evidence.shows: Claude Opus 4.6 autonomously reimplemented the tested functionality of gotree, a bioinformatics toolkit. It passed 1,899 visible tests and 101 of 102 hidden tests, investigated failures, and corrected its own parser. The researchers considered the task effectively solved, while noting mixed code quality and uncertainty in the human-time estimates.

evidence.item: METR announcement of MirrorCode preliminary results
evidence.shows: METR identified the result as evidence of weeks-long coding tasks, in a project it funded and co-developed with Epoch AI.

evidence.item: Frontier Risk Report
evidence.shows: On the early MirrorCode suite, METR estimated Opus 4.6's time horizon at more than 100 human hours, while finding substantially shorter horizons on its broader task suite.

evidence.item: MirrorCode benchmark paper
evidence.shows: A later Opus 4.7 run substantially reimplemented gotree in 14 hours, passing 2,000 of 2,001 tests; the paper emphasizes that performance is strongest when requirements are precisely specified.

SA-015.thesis: By 2027, an AI agent will be able to join a company as a drop-in remote worker, acquire the company-specific context a new human hire needs, and participate in ordinary workplace communication and software workflows.
indicatorsYes: An AI agent can be onboarded into a company's work using relevant internal context and apply that context usefully in its work.
An onboarded agent can communicate with colleagues through ordinary workplace channels as part of its work.
An onboarded agent can use the company's ordinary software and tools to participate in its workflows.
indicatorsNo: AI agents still cannot acquire and use the company-specific context needed to contribute as onboarded coworkers.
AI agents remain confined to isolated interactions and cannot participate in ordinary workplace communication and software workflows.
SA-015.reasoning: The documented systems meet the fixed indicators: they can be given company context, apply it to work, communicate in Slack, and use connected tools in workplace workflows. Claude Tag's June 2026 launch and reported internal use provide a concrete example combining those capabilities, making that the first demonstrated date used here, though an earlier date is possible. The evidence includes vendor reports and does not establish unrestricted human-level reliability; METR's findings qualify confidence but the fixed reading does not require that standard.

evidence.item: Codex became generally available with a Slack integration.
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported that colleagues could delegate tasks to Codex in a Slack thread; it gathered conversational context, worked in a coding environment, and returned a completed task for people to review or continue. OpenAI also described its use in company code-review and code-cleanup workflows.

evidence.item: METR published its February–March 2026 frontier risk report.
evidence.shows: Some companies confirmed that agents often autonomously wrote complex pull requests, analyzed data, and performed other technical work. METR also found substantial weaknesses in judgment and reliability and a gap between benchmark performance and real-world performance.

evidence.item: OpenAI described Codex use across workplace roles and tools.
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported that Zapier teams used Codex to draw on Slack, Google Docs, and Coda knowledge to produce postmortems, incident-response plans, and feature tickets. This is evidence of company-specific context being applied to ordinary work.

evidence.item: Anthropic launched Claude Tag in beta for Enterprise and Team customers.
evidence.shows: Anthropic reported that teams could add Claude to Slack, grant it access to selected channels, tools, data and codebases, and delegate tasks to it. It described Claude retaining channel context, responding to colleagues, using connected tools and working asynchronously; Anthropic reported using its internal version for coding, product metrics and support work.

SA-016.thesis: A drop-in remote AI worker would be dramatically easier to integrate into work than intermediate models. It is plausible that, because integrating those earlier models takes longer, economic value generated by AI would rise somewhat discontinuously when drop-in workers become available.
SA-016.condition: By the time the drop-in remote worker is able to automate a large number of jobs, intermediate models won’t yet have been fully harnessed and integrated.
SA-016.horizon: Conditional on the availability of a drop-in remote worker capable of automating a large number of jobs; no separate fixed date is specified for the economic jump.
indicatorsYes: Organizations can integrate drop-in remote AI workers into relevant jobs with dramatically less workflow change and integration work than intermediate models require.
When drop-in workers become capable of automating a large number of jobs, substantial potential value from intermediate models remains unrealized because integration is incomplete.
Economic value generated by AI rises markedly and somewhat discontinuously around the adoption of drop-in remote workers.
indicatorsNo: Drop-in remote workers require as much or more workflow change and integration work to generate value as intermediate models.
Despite the stated condition being met, economic value generated by AI continues to grow smoothly, with no discernible jump associated with drop-in workers.
SA-016.reasoning: The available evidence does not establish that a drop-in remote worker capable of automating a large number of jobs has arrived, so the condition concerning the state of intermediate-model integration at that time remains pending. Integration costs and limited realized productivity effects are consistent with the proposed mechanism, but they do not establish the required comparison or an economic-value jump. The 0.1 credence estimates that the thesis has already come true; the claim has no separate fixed deadline for the jump.
SA-016.measure: Economic value generated by AI models; no unit or numerical threshold is specified for this claim.
SA-016.measureUsed: AI-generated economic value has no specified unit or numerical threshold. Relevant evidence includes professional-standard completion of remote freelance projects, firm-reported productivity effects, and the costs of integrating AI into workflows; these are indicators, not a combined estimate of total AI-generated value.

evidence.item: Remote Labor Index results
evidence.shows: The best agent tested completed 15.8% of the benchmark's freelance projects to at least the professional deliverable standard, up from 2.5% for the best agent at the benchmark's release. This shows progress on economically valuable work, but projects are not complete jobs and the result does not establish a broadly deployable drop-in worker.

evidence.item: Frontier Risk Report, assessing models in February–March 2026
evidence.shows: METR's best measured 50% task-completion horizon among shared models was below 20 hours, with substantial measurement uncertainty near that range. The benchmark covers software tasks and does not establish performance across whole remote jobs.

evidence.item: The AI Buildout and the Economy
evidence.shows: Federal Reserve researchers say moving from isolated tasks to complete workflows often requires costly integration into firm-specific systems, while aggregate output and labor data showed limited signs of broad-based transformation.

evidence.item: Global Evidence on Business Use of AI
evidence.shows: In a survey conducted from November 2025 to January 2026, 89% of surveyed executives reported no AI effect on their firms' labor productivity over the preceding three years. This is evidence of limited realized firm-level effects, not a direct measurement of unrealized potential.

SA-017.thesis: By 2025–2026, AI machines that can think and reason will broadly outperform many college graduates.
indicatorsYes: By the end of 2026, AI systems demonstrate thinking and reasoning across a broad range of tasks at a level exceeding that of many college graduates.
Comparative evaluations across varied tasks show AI systems outperforming many college graduates overall.
indicatorsNo: By the end of 2026, AI systems do not demonstrate broad thinking and reasoning performance that exceeds that of many college graduates.
Comparative evaluations across varied tasks show AI systems generally performing below college graduates, with superior performance confined to narrow areas.
SA-017.reasoning: By late 2025, comparative cognitive assessments showed AI outperforming human groups across several reasoning-related domains, including postgraduates on one test; work-task and benchmark evidence supports a broader capability assessment. Together, these results substantiate the reading's comparison with many graduates, though no cited study directly measures a representative sample of graduates across all real-world activities. The resolution date is the publication date of the comparative study used to establish the verdict, not a claim that this was the earliest possible demonstration. Uneven performance on practical tasks and limitations of structured tests reduce confidence but do not require adding a universal competence threshold.

evidence.item: A comparative study evaluated o1-preview against human participants on established assessments spanning several higher-order cognitive domains.
evidence.shows: The model exceeded undergraduate and postgraduate comparison scores on a critical-thinking essay test and scored above human comparison groups on several other assessments, including systematic thinking, data literacy, creative thinking, logical reasoning and scientific reasoning. The authors also reported limitations in problem-solving and adaptive reasoning.

evidence.item: OpenAI's GDPval evaluated 220 work tasks across 44 occupations using blinded comparisons with experienced professionals' deliverables.
evidence.shows: The best model in the initial evaluation, Claude Opus 4.1, was rated as good as or better than experts on just under half the tasks. The evaluation provides broad practical evidence, although it tests one-shot deliverables rather than complete jobs or interactive workflows.

evidence.item: Stanford's 2026 AI Index reviewed AI performance against human baselines across multiple benchmark categories.
evidence.shows: Frontier systems met or exceeded established human baselines on several long-running benchmarks, including MMLU, while performance remained below human baselines on some autonomous software engineering and computer-use measures. The report cautions that structured benchmarks do not capture the full breadth of real-world capabilities.

evidence.item: METR ran a randomized trial involving 16 experienced open-source developers and 246 tasks using early-2025 AI tools.
evidence.shows: Allowing AI tools increased task completion time by an estimated 19% in this particular setting, illustrating a practical limitation rather than a direct test of AI versus graduates overall.

SA-018.thesis: In the illustrative 2027–2028 trajectory, proto-automated AI researchers can automate more than 90% of the work of AI researchers and engineers, though some human bottlenecks remain.
indicatorsYes: By 2028, evidence shows AI systems can perform more than 90% of AI research and engineering work, measured across the relevant work of researchers and engineers.
AI systems can carry out the research cycle: engage with ML literature, develop questions or ideas, implement experiments, and interpret results, with human involvement confined to a small remainder.
indicatorsNo: By the end of 2028, evidence shows AI systems can automate no more than 90% of AI research and engineering work.
AI systems remain unable to carry out enough of the research cycle for their automatable share of the work to exceed 90%.
SA-018.reasoning: The evidence shows substantial and rapidly growing AI participation in research, but it does not establish that systems can automate more than 90% of the relevant work with human involvement confined to a small remainder. Anthropic's over-90% collaboration figure includes close human direction and therefore cannot be equated with the forecast's threshold. The window remains open through 2028; rapid recent progress supports an on-track judgment, but extrapolating to the threshold is uncertain.
SA-018.measure: Percentage of AI researcher and engineer work that proto-automated AI researchers can automate; the author does not specify a measurement method.
SA-018.measureUsed: Share of the work of AI researchers and engineers at leading labs that AI systems can perform, allowing a small human remainder and some supervision. No available estimate directly measures that share. Anthropic's August 2026 index estimates that AI leads 26% of its weighted model R&D work and collaborates or leads on over 90%; these are measures of observed involvement, not estimates of the share that could be automated. OpenAI reports 3.1 agent-workdays per human workday in mid-August 2026, a usage measure rather than a share of work automated. METR's approximately 1.9× capability-benchmark acceleration through October 2026 is a progress-rate estimate, not an automation percentage.

evidence.item: Anthropic's R&D Automation Index
evidence.shows: Anthropic estimates that Claude led 26% of its weighted AI R&D work, meaning it completed most of a task from a high-level prompt under human supervision. AI collaborated or led on over 90%, but collaboration includes large chunks of work under close human direction. The index uses a model-judged, person-time-weighted task basket and does not directly establish the automatable share.

evidence.item: Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported 3.1 agent-workdays per human workday in its research organization in mid-August. It also reported that agents still needed significant human steering, particularly on more complex tasks, and that high-level planning was a minimal fraction of agent output tokens.

evidence.item: Two shadow evaluations of open-ended AI research
evidence.shows: Agents completed the engineering in two research case studies without human help but did not make substantial progress on the central research questions. This is direct evidence of uneven capabilities, although two cases cannot establish the overall automatable share.

evidence.item: Independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic
evidence.shows: METR estimated that Anthropic's model benchmark scores had advanced at roughly 1.9 times their earlier rate, with substantial uncertainty. It reported that AI accelerated R&D primarily through assistance and was not yet making highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of model training; much relevant evidence was redacted.

SA-019.thesis: In the illustrative 2027–2028 trajectory, partial automation of AI research already accelerates the pace of AI progress by at least threefold, despite remaining human and coordination bottlenecks.
SA-019.condition: In the illustrative trajectory, proto-automated researchers can automate more than 90% of research work, while some human and coordination bottlenecks remain.
indicatorsYes: By 2027–2028, AI systems are doing a substantial share of AI research work and contributing to advances while some human involvement remains.
The pace of relevant AI research progress is at least three times its prior pace, with partial research automation contributing to the acceleration.
indicatorsNo: By the end of 2028, AI research progress has not accelerated to at least three times its prior pace.
By the end of 2028, AI research progress has accelerated at least threefold, but partial research automation has not contributed to that acceleration.
SA-019.reasoning: The window is still open, and the strongest available direct assessment estimates about 2× progress, rather than establishing at least 3×, although its uncertainty extends to 3×. Substantial AI involvement and AI-attributed acceleration before 2027 put the trajectory ahead, but the stated condition of proto-researchers capable of automating more than 90% of research work remains pending. The proxy measures capabilities at one lab and cannot precisely establish the rate of AI research progress across the field.
SA-019.measure: Rate of AI research progress, expressed as a multiple of the prior pace. The author's related benchmark for algorithmic efficiency is approximately 0.5 orders of magnitude of effective compute per year, excluding additional unhobbling gains.
SA-019.measureUsed: Rate of AI capability progress relative to an earlier rate, with AI research automation contributing. As a proxy, METR estimated in October 2026 that Anthropic’s progress on well-specified model tasks was about 2× its March 2024–October 2025 rate; its measured benchmark-index growth ratio was 1.9×, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.5–2.8×. METR considered a rate as high as 3× plausible but uncertain. Separately, Epoch AI’s March 2024 estimate for pretraining algorithmic efficiency was a compute-equivalent doubling every 8 months, or approximately 0.45 orders of magnitude per year; that historical benchmark is not a measurement of current acceleration.

evidence.item: Independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic
evidence.shows: METR estimated roughly 2× historical capability-progress speed as of October 2026, with substantial uncertainty, and judged that AI use in R&D likely accounted for a majority of the acceleration. Its benchmark-index estimate was 1.9× with a 95% confidence interval of 1.5–2.8×. Much of the evidence METR considered most informative was redacted.

evidence.item: Anthropic R&D Automation Index snapshot
evidence.shows: Anthropic reported that Claude led 26% of measured AI R&D work and collaborated or led on over 90%, with humans still involved. Collaboration on over 90% is not the same measure as automating over 90% of the work.

evidence.item: Research acceleration inside OpenAI
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported 3.1 agent-workdays per human workday in its research organization by mid-August, increased experiments per researcher, and continued need for human steering. Agent runtime is not itself a measure of research progress or productivity.

evidence.item: Algorithmic progress in language models
evidence.shows: Epoch estimated that compute needed for a given pretrained language-model performance level historically halved roughly every eight months, with a 95% confidence interval of five to fourteen months.

SA-020.thesis: Once AI systems can replace most AI researcher and engineer work but still have blind spots or need some human supervision, the remaining steps to fully automate that work will take no more than a few years.
SA-020.condition: AI systems can already replace most AI researcher and engineer work, but still have blind spots or require some human supervision.
SA-020.horizon: Within a few years after partial automation
indicatorsYes: Within a few years of systems reaching the partial-automation stage, AI systems can perform the full range of AI researcher and engineer work without the remaining human supervision being necessary.
Previously unautomated research and engineering tasks or blind spots cease to require human researchers or engineers for the work to be completed.
indicatorsNo: More than a few years after the partial-automation stage, AI researcher and engineer work still cannot be fully automated.
Remaining tasks or blind spots continue to require human researchers or engineers beyond a few years after partial automation.
SA-020.reasoning: As of November 15, 2026, the evidence shows substantial assistance and some supervised delegation, but does not establish that AI can replace most AI researcher and engineer work. The conditional clock therefore has no defensible start date, and the transition time cannot yet be graded; the small credence reflects uncertainty that the thesis has already been fulfilled, not a forecast conditional on a future start. Neither the absence of a demonstrated full transition nor the illustrative 2027–2028 trajectory establishes failure.
SA-020.measure: Elapsed time in years from the partial-automation stage to full automation of AI researcher and engineer work.
SA-020.measureUsed: Elapsed years between AI systems being able to replace most AI researcher and engineer work, with blind spots or some human supervision remaining, and their being able to perform the full range without that remaining supervision. No defensible start or end date is established. For consistency with SA-018, AI collaboration on a task is not treated as replacement of that task.

evidence.item: Anthropic R&D Automation Index
evidence.shows: As of August, Claude led 26% of measured model R&D work under human supervision and collaborated on over 90%; it was not rated fully autonomous on any measured subset. The index measures actual work at one lab and has methodological limitations, but collaboration is not equivalent to replacing most research work.

evidence.item: Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported an automated research intern capable of well-defined tasks under human direction. Humans still set research priorities and judge which ideas and results to pursue; more than half of successful four-to-eight-hour tasks involved at least one intervention.

evidence.item: Independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic
evidence.shows: After an assessment through October 29, METR reported that Anthropic's R&D was accelerated primarily by AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions. Its acceleration estimates were uncertain and some evidence was redacted.

evidence.item: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
evidence.shows: In two shadow evaluations, frontier agents completed the engineering without human help but did not make substantial progress on the open-ended research questions. This is evidence of remaining blind spots, though only for two research projects.

SA-021.thesis: Once AI research is fully automated and compute supports a large population of effective automated researchers, their work will probably compress about a human decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less.
SA-021.condition: After full AI research automation, compute supports large populations of effective automated researchers.
SA-021.horizon: Approximately one year after full AI research automation, given the stated compute condition.
indicatorsYes: A large population of effective automated AI researchers conducts AI research using available inference and experiment compute.

Within approximately a year, AI research produces algorithmic efficiency gains equivalent to at least 5 orders of magnitude of effective compute, or roughly a decade at the author's stated historical rate.
The automated research effort materially contributes to that acceleration, including through whatever combination of methods proves effective.
indicatorsNo: After full automation and with compute supporting a large population of effective automated researchers, algorithmic efficiency gains over approximately a year fall substantially short of 5 orders of magnitude.
Automated researchers make little contribution to accelerating algorithmic progress, for example because experiment-compute bottlenecks or diminishing returns keep progress near its previous pace.
SA-021.reasoning: As of 2026-11-15, there is substantial AI assistance and some autonomous work in AI R&D, but the available evidence does not establish that AI research is fully automated or that compute supports the postulated population of effective automated researchers. The condition is therefore not met and the approximately one-year conditional window has not begun. METR’s evidence of acceleration is meaningful but does not establish the specified 100,000× annual algorithmic efficiency gain; the credence refers to the chance that the thesis has already come true, despite incomplete public evidence.
SA-021.measure: Algorithmic efficiency gains expressed as orders of magnitude of effective compute: 5 or more orders of magnitude in approximately one year, compared with the author's estimated historical trend of 0.5 orders of magnitude per year.
SA-021.measureUsed: The target is at least 5 orders of magnitude, or 100,000×, in algorithmic effective compute in approximately one year, attributable materially to automated research. Epoch AI’s historical pretraining estimate, published 2024-03-12, was a doubling every 8 months, approximately 0.45 orders of magnitude per year; this is a baseline estimate, not a measurement of progress in 2026. METR’s approximately 2× acceleration estimate for October 2026 concerns model capability progress and cannot be equated to a measured annual gain in algorithmic effective compute.

evidence.item: Anthropic’s R&D Automation Index and agent count
evidence.shows: Anthropic reported about 30,000 agents doing research and engineering work simultaneously on its most-used internal platform. Claude led 26% of measured AI R&D work under supervision, but was not fully autonomous for any measured subset.

evidence.item: Independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
evidence.shows: METR estimated that model capability progress on well-specified tasks was roughly twice its earlier rate, with substantial uncertainty, and found evidence of significant AI contribution. It also reported that AI was not yet making highly significant fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of model training. Detailed algorithmic progress estimates were not publicly disclosed.

evidence.item: Research acceleration at OpenAI
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported an automated research intern that handles well-defined tasks under human direction and described an automated AI researcher as a future goal.

evidence.item: Historical algorithmic progress in language models
evidence.shows: Epoch estimated that pretraining compute required for a given performance level halved approximately every 8 months, with a 95% interval of 5 to 14 months. Its analysis did not cover post-training gains.

SA-022.thesis: After AI fully automates frontier AI research, progress will take AI from that level to vastly superhuman systems within a few years. These systems will be qualitatively smarter than humans, capable of novel, creative and complex intellectual work far beyond human abilities.
SA-022.condition: Fully automated frontier AI research is achieved.
SA-022.horizon: After fully automated frontier AI research: about one year, or at most a few years.
indicatorsYes: Within a few years of full frontier AI research automation, AI systems demonstrate intellectual performance vastly beyond the best humans across many domains.
Within that period, AI systems produce novel, creative solutions to extremely difficult scientific or technological problems that humans would otherwise be stuck on for decades.

Within that period, AI systems demonstrate complex reasoning or produce work substantially beyond human understanding, consistent with qualitative superiority rather than merely greater speed or scale.
indicatorsNo: A few years after full frontier AI research automation, available evidence shows no AI systems with intellectual capabilities vastly beyond the best humans across many domains.
A few years after full frontier AI research automation, AI systems remain primarily human-level or only modestly superhuman, with no evidence of the predicted qualitative leap.
SA-022.reasoning: As of 2026-11-15, available evidence shows meaningful automation and acceleration of AI research, but does not establish that frontier AI research has been fully automated. The condition is therefore not met, and the few-year window has not started; this is not a failure verdict on the subsequent transition. The 0.05 credence is a subjective probability that the conditioned thesis has already come true, reflecting uncertainty about private capabilities and the precise point of full automation.
SA-022.measure: Elapsed time in years from fully automated frontier AI research to vastly superhuman AI systems; qualitative intellectual capability relative to humans across domains.
SA-022.measureUsed: Full frontier AI research automation means AI can carry out the frontier AI research process without the human research contributions needed to advance it; the elapsed-time clock starts when that condition is achieved. Qualitative capability is assessed across intellectual domains, not by speed or scale alone. No start date can yet be established.

evidence.item: METR's high-access assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic
evidence.shows: METR estimated that model capability progress on well-specified tasks was roughly twice its earlier rate, with substantial uncertainty, and attributed a majority of the acceleration to AI use in R&D. The assessment describes further automation as a potential future source of acceleration; much of the most informative evidence was redacted.

evidence.item: METR September progress report
evidence.shows: On one AI R&D challenge, METR estimated that AI agents outperformed human experts at budgets below approximately $3,000 but underperformed on larger-scale work. The estimate was sensitive to the amount of human labor assumed.

evidence.item: The AI Scientist end-to-end research pipeline
evidence.shows: An AI research system generated ideas, ran experiments and wrote a manuscript that passed the first review round at a workshop. This is evidence of progress in automating research workflows, but does not establish full automation of frontier AI research.

evidence.item: Benchmarking AI scientists for biological discovery
evidence.shows: The benchmark authors found that evaluated systems fell short of fully autonomous biological discovery, while the best performed comparably to graduate-level researchers on their scientific discovery task.

evidence.item: Microsoft's fiscal 2025 first-quarter earnings call

evidence.item: Microsoft's fiscal 2025 second-quarter earnings release

evidence.item: OpenAI annualized revenue report

SA-045.thesis: If OpenAI’s roughly six-month revenue-doubling trend continues, its revenue should reach approximately a $10 billion annual run rate by late 2024 or early 2025.
indicatorsYes: A reported or disclosed OpenAI revenue run rate is approximately $10 billion per year by late 2024 or early 2025.

indicatorsNo: By early 2025, reliable reported or disclosed figures put OpenAI’s annual revenue run rate substantially below approximately $10 billion.

OpenAI reached the stated scale by June 2025, later than the forecast window, supporting Partly. Epoch's April projection leaves some uncertainty about how close the run rate was near the end of early 2025; June is the first reported $10 billion observation found, not necessarily the exact first date reached.
SA-045.measure: OpenAI revenue annual run rate, in US dollars per year
SA-045.measureUsed: OpenAI's own annualized revenue run rate in US dollars per year, including consumer products, business ChatGPT products and API usage, but not Microsoft's separate AI revenue. OpenAI reported approximately $5.5 billion for December 2024 and $10 billion by June 2025. Epoch AI projected approximately $10 billion for April 2025; that projection is an estimate, not a disclosed observation.

evidence.item: Epoch AI estimated OpenAI revenue at around $10 billion per year by projecting reported revenue trends to April 2025.
